## Big Idea

- A ring width is a sum of parts: the tree's size and age, that year's weather, disturbance to the tree or its neighbors, and noise. You never see them separately. Keep Andy's opening sentences.
- Fix the arithmetic analogy so it points where the chapter goes. One total of 10 can't tell you whether it was 3+2+4+1 or 1+4+6-1. But forty totals that share some of their terms can be solved for those terms, and that is what a collection is: forty cores, two from each tree, all from one stand. Sampling design is how the parts get pulled apart. The catch, which the chapter comes back to, is two terms that always turn up together.
- Methods tell the parts apart by two things: who shares a part (one core, one tree, or the whole stand) and how fast it changes (year to year, or over decades). Every method in the book is after one part, and it mistakes another part for it when the two match on both counts.
- To see that you need a collection where the parts are known, so the chapter builds one. Keep the simulation paragraph and the [@Bunn2004] line.
- Promise: by the end you know the parts, how the simulated stand is built, and what each method in the book is after and can be fooled by.

## How Fast It Changes

- New section, the second sort. The age trend and competition change over decades. Climate and noise change from year to year, with a year or two of memory. Disturbances arrive in one year and fade over years (the stand event) to decades (the release). Use the SIM10A figure again, reading it for speed this time.
- A small table, parts by who shares them and how fast they change. This is the table every method in the book can be placed on.
- A filter is the tool for sorting by speed, and the [aside that follows](02xAsideFiltering.qmd) takes it up. One or two sentences only.

## What Each Method Is After

- Rebuild the old closing table (method, part it is after, what it can mistake for that part, where in the book) as the center of the chapter, placed on the who-shares and how-fast table:
  - Crossdating keeps what is shared and fast. In raw widths the age trend looks shared (every tree slopes downhill), which is why the dating tools filter first.
  - Detrending removes what belongs to one tree and changes slowly, so it can take competition with the age trend, or a slow swing in climate.
  - A chronology keeps what is shared, so it can't tell climate from a stand-wide disturbance.
  - A tree series (`treeMean`) keeps what belongs to one tree, which is where a release shows.
- One worked example, the stand event of 1880, because it shows the model's limit in a single figure: a chronology can't tell $D2_t$ from $C_t$ without knowing which trees were hit. Keep the two-panel figure (or panel A only), the Douglass condition (many trees, a wide area, a long time), Cook's three hemlocks, and Wigley et al. and Buras on EPS. Decide in the draft whether the 1870s spline lift stays here or goes to [Detrending](08Detrending.qmd), which already calls it "chapter 2's puzzle".
- Keep Cook's "one researcher's 'signal' will frequently be another researcher's 'noise'" [@Cook1987, p. 38], and the climate and ecology views of the same parts. A record is good for a purpose.
